x-m-e3-01.title: Different Ways to Share 72 Candies Equally Among Plates
x-m-e3-01.goal: Find several ways to share that meet the conditions (the range for the number of plates and the number of candies on each plate) at the same time, and explain how the number of plates and the number of candies on one plate pair up.
x-m-e3-01.material: You want to put 72 candies on plates, sharing them equally with none left over. The number of candies on each plate changes depending on how many plates you use.
x-m-e3-01.thinking.0: Finding several ways that meet the conditions at the same time
x-m-e3-01.thinking.1: Checking candidates by multiplying and sorting the ones that work from the ones that do not
x-m-e3-01.thinking.2: Finding the pattern: what happens to one number when the other gets bigger
x-m-e3-01.prereq.0: Can read a multiplication table (you may use the table while solving)
x-m-e3-01.prereq.1: Can explain in words a situation of sharing equally
x-m-e3-01.s.s1.prompt: From the choices for the number of plates, choose all the numbers of plates that let you share 72 candies equally with none left over.
x-m-e3-01.s.s1.r.b: The multiples of 5 skip past it: 70, 75. Being close to 72 does not mean the candies can be shared with none left over.
x-m-e3-01.s.s1.r.d: The multiples of 7 skip past it: 70, 77. If you guessed it works because the number is even, check the products yourself.
x-m-e3-01.s.s1.explain: You can share the candies equally with none left over only when the number of plates times the number of candies on one plate is 72. 4×18, 6×12, and 9×8 are 72, and no number multiplied by 5 or 7 makes 72.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.prompt: You will use at least 2 and at most 9 plates, and you want to put more than 10 candies on each plate. Make 3 ways with different numbers of plates so that the 72 candies are shared equally with none left over.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one that the pair you found follows both conditions (the range for the number of plates, and more than 10 candies).
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.var.b: Number of candies on one plate
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of plates and the number of candies as natural numbers.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of plates is at least 2 and at most 9.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of plates is not between 2 and 9.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.ok.c3: You put more than 10 candies on each plate.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.fail.c3: You need to put more than 10 candies on each plate.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.ok.c4: Number of plates × number of candies is 72.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Number of plates × number of candies is not 72. Multiply again.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.explain: 2×36, 3×24, 4×18, and 6×12 are all 72. With 8 or 9 plates, each plate would get fewer than 10 candies, which does not meet the conditions.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Look at your ways side by side. As the number of plates goes up, what happens to the number of candies on one plate? Write your answer using the numbers you made.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write your ways in order, starting from the smallest number of plates.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare one after another how the number of plates changes and how the number of candies changes.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: When the plates go from 2 to 3, ...
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you actually mention a pair of numbers you made (for example, 2 plates and 36 candies)?
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect it to the fact that the number of plates times the number of candies is always 72?
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.model.0: As the number of plates goes 2, 3, 4, the number of candies on one plate goes down 36, 24, 18. Multiplying the two always gives 72.
x-m-e3-01.s.s2.because.model.1: If you use more plates, each plate holds fewer candies. With 3 plates it was 24 candies, and with 6 plates it is 12.

x-m-e3-02.title: Finding the Mistake in Seoyeon's Candy Sharing
x-m-e3-02.goal: Use the condition that the remainder must be smaller than the divisor to find and fix the error in a solution, and tell apart the cases where the same error happens and where it does not.
x-m-e3-02.material: Seoyeon wants to share 85 candies equally among 4 people. Read Seoyeon's solution. The quotient is the number each person gets, and the remainder is the number left over after sharing.
x-m-e3-02.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
x-m-e3-02.thinking.1: Explaining the reason for the error using a condition (comparing the remainder with the divisor)
x-m-e3-02.thinking.2: Making and checking an example that fits the condition
x-m-e3-02.prereq.0: Can read a situation with a remainder after sharing equally as a number sentence (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Seoyeon's solution that is hard to believe.
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.hint.1: Read from line 1 in order and find the first line where what it says stops being right.
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.line.1: If you subtract 80 from 85, 5 is left.
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.line.2: The leftover 5 cannot be shared any more, so 85÷4=20 ··· 5.
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.line.3: Check: 4×20+5=85, so the number sentence fits together.
x-m-e3-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The 5 leftover candies can be shared again, 1 more candy to each of the 4 people, so saying 'cannot be shared any more' is not right. The check in line 4 only shows that the number sentence fits together; it does not tell you whether the remainder is correct.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.prompt: You shared the candies equally among 4 people, and each person got 20 candies with some candies left over. Find and write 2 possible numbers for how many candies there were at the start.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.hint.0: If each person gets 20 candies, first find how many candies the 4 people got in all.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Work out how many more candies there must be than that, and how many can be left over without being able to share one more time.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.var.n: Number of candies at the start
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of candies as a natural number.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The number each person gets is not 20. Share among 4 people and check the quotient again.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.fail.c3: There are no candies left over. There must be some left over.
x-m-e3-02.s.s2.explain: 81, 82, or 83 candies are possible. If 4 or more candies are left over, each person can get 1 more candy, so the number each person gets would not be 20.
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.prompt: Tell Seoyeon the correct quotient and remainder of 85÷4. Also write the reason why 5 left over is or is not okay.
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check that your corrected answer makes 4×(quotient)+(remainder)=85.
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check the corrected quotient and remainder (21 and 1) like 4×21+1=85?
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why the remainder must be smaller than the divisor?
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.model.0: 85÷4=21 ··· 1. There were 5 left over, but you can give 1 more to each of the 4 people, so it can be shared more. The remainder must be smaller than the divisor 4.
x-m-e3-02.s.s3.model.1: If you give each person 21 candies, 4×21=84 and 1 is left over. The remainder 5 is bigger than 4, so it can be shared one more time, which means Seoyeon's answer is wrong.

x-m-e3-03.title: Are the Fraction 8/10 m and the Decimal 0.8 m the Same Length?
x-m-e3-03.goal: Use the evidence of the same tape measure marks to compare lengths written as a fraction and as a decimal, and apply that evidence to explain a comparison of two new numbers.
x-m-e3-03.material: A tape measure 1 m long is divided into 10 equal spaces. The length of one space is 1/10 m (one tenth of a meter), and in decimals you write it as 0.1 m. The blue string is as long as 8 spaces of the tape measure, and in fractions it is 8/10 m (eight tenths of a meter). The length of the green string is 0.8 m.
x-m-e3-03.thinking.0: Comparing and judging claims in light of evidence
x-m-e3-03.thinking.1: Explaining by giving a reason (the number of marked spaces)
x-m-e3-03.thinking.2: Applying the reason you found to a new situation
x-m-e3-03.prereq.0: Can read what fractions with denominator 10 and decimals with one decimal place show (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.prompt: Three friends compared the lengths of the blue string and the green string. Whose statement fits the information above best?
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find in the information how many spaces of the tape measure each of the blue string and the green string covers, and compare them.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check in the information how 'one space' is written as a fraction and as a decimal.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.o.a: Doyun: Fractions and decimals are different kinds of numbers, so you cannot compare lengths.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.r.a: This judged only by the fact that the names of the numbers are different. Check what happens when you mark them on the marks of the same tape measure.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.o.b: Seoa: One space is 0.1 m, so both strings are 8 spaces and have the same length.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.r.b: This used the number of marked spaces in the information as the reason.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.o.c: Hajun: 0.8 m is longer. A number with a decimal point is measured more accurately.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.r.c: This judged by a feeling of 'accurate.' Find in the information how many spaces each string is and compare them.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.o.d: Jiu: 8/10 m is longer. It has two numbers in it, so it looks bigger.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.r.d: How many numbers are written has nothing to do with length. How many spaces it covers on the tape measure is the reason.
x-m-e3-03.s.s1.explain: One space is 1/10 m and also 0.1 m. The length of 8 spaces is 8/10 m written as a fraction and 0.8 m written as a decimal, so it is the same length written in two ways.
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.prompt: This time there is a 0.3 m string and a 4/10 m string (four tenths of a meter). Which one is longer? Use the tape measure marks to write your reason.
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many spaces on the tape measure 0.3 m and 4/10 m each cover.
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the numbers of spaces you counted and make a sentence giving your reason.
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: ... is longer. This is because ...
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many spaces each of the two strings covers on the tape measure?
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain using the marks, not 'because it is a decimal' or 'because the number is bigger'?
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.model.0: 4/10 m is longer. One space is 0.1 m, and 0.3 m is 3 spaces while 4/10 m is 4 spaces, so 4 spaces is longer.
x-m-e3-03.s.s2.model.1: 0.3 m is 3 spaces on the tape measure, and 4/10 m is 4 marked spaces. So 0.3 m is shorter than 4/10 m, and 4/10 m is longer.

x-m-e3-04.title: Pizza Slices 1/3 and 1/6: Which Is Bigger?
x-m-e3-04.goal: Check your judgment about the size of fractions each time new information is revealed, and state the condition that the whole must be the same size in order to compare the sizes of fractions.
x-m-e3-04.material: A pizza shop cuts pizzas into equal pieces and sells them. The information is revealed one step at a time. At each step, choose the best idea given what you know right now.
x-m-e3-04.thinking.0: Revising your judgment as new information comes
x-m-e3-04.thinking.1: Finding the condition for comparing the sizes of fractions
x-m-e3-04.thinking.2: Stating the condition under which a generalization holds
x-m-e3-04.prereq.0: Can read one part of a whole divided equally as a fraction (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.prompt: Look at the information one piece at a time and see whether there is any judgment you should change.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first check whether the two pieces you want to compare come from pizzas of the same size.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether the conclusion you made in an earlier step can still be used with the new information.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.info: There are two pizzas of the same size. One is cut into 3 equal pieces, and the other is cut into 6 equal pieces. One piece of the pizza cut into 3 is 1/3 (one third) of the whole, and one piece of the pizza cut into 6 is 1/6 (one sixth).
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which side has the bigger piece?
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.after: When pizzas of the same size are cut, a piece from the pizza cut into 3 is bigger than a piece from the pizza cut into 6. So at this step, the 1/3 piece is bigger.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: One piece of the pizza cut into 6
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You may have thought that because 6 is a bigger number than 3, the piece is bigger. Think about what happens to one piece when the same pizza is cut into more pieces.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: One piece of the pizza cut into 3
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This choice thought about how, when pizzas of the same size are cut into fewer pieces, one piece is bigger.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The two pieces are the same size
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You may have looked only at both numerators being 1. Also look at the number of pieces each pizza is cut into.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.info: New information: The second shop has a big pizza and a small pizza. One big pizza is the same amount as 6 small pizzas. Compare one piece (1/6) of the big pizza cut into 6 equal pieces with one piece (1/3) of the small pizza cut into 3 equal pieces.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: This time, which piece is bigger?
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The 1/6 piece of the big pizza is the same amount as one whole small pizza, and the 1/3 piece of the small pizza is less than one whole small pizza. When the wholes are different sizes, a piece with a smaller fraction can still be bigger.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The 1/3 piece of the small pizza
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This choice carried over what you just found, '1/3 is bigger than 1/6,' as it was. First check whether the two pizzas are the same size.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The 1/6 piece of the big pizza
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This choice compared the amount of one big pizza with the small pizza.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: You cannot tell from the fractions alone
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This choice thought about how, when the wholes are different, it is hard to say the size of the pieces from the fractions alone.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: Dohyeon said, 'Since 1/3 is bigger than 1/6, a 1/3 piece is always bigger no matter which pizza it is.'
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: For Dohyeon's statement to hold, what has to be the same?
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.after: You can compare the sizes of 1/3 and 1/6 by their denominators only when the wholes are the same size. So Dohyeon's statement is right only with the condition 'if the pizzas are the same size.'
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If the number of pieces were the same, the denominators would be the same, so the situation you want to compare would change. Check again whether this is the condition you need right now.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The numerators of the two fractions are already the same, 1. Even so, the result was different at the second shop.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The size of the whole pizza before it is cut
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This choice recalled what made your judgment change at the second shop.
x-m-e3-04.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked as if you could compare by the denominators alone, but when a situation with wholes of different sizes came up, you had to change your judgment. Think back to which piece of information made you change your judgment.
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.prompt: Write what you would tell Dohyeon. Write which of 1/3 and 1/6 is bigger, and what has to be the same for you to be able to say so.
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think back to what the reason was that the result changed at the second shop.
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write one sentence each: which of 1/3 and 1/6 is bigger, and the condition under which you can say so.
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Dohyeon, if the pizzas are the same size, ...
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the condition 'the whole must be the same size' in your own words?
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write it thinking about the example of the second shop (the big pizza and the small pizza)?
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.model.0: 1/3 is bigger than 1/6 only when you cut pizzas of the same size. If the wholes are different sizes, you cannot tell the size of the pieces from the fractions alone.
x-m-e3-04.s.s2.model.1: If the pizzas are the same size, one piece when cut into 3 equal parts, 1/3, is bigger than one piece when cut into 6 equal parts, 1/6. But with a big pizza and a small pizza, it can be different.

x-m-e3-05.title: How Can You Find the Radius of One Cookie?
x-m-e3-05.goal: Tell apart the information that lets you solve the problem from the information that does not matter, use the relationship between the diameter and the radius of a circle to find the answer, and then make other cases under the same condition.
x-m-e3-05.material: 3 round cookies of the same size are placed in a row across a rectangular box. What is the radius of one cookie in cm?
x-m-e3-05.thinking.0: Sorting out the information you need from the information you do not need
x-m-e3-05.thinking.1: Finding and checking a value using enough information
x-m-e3-05.thinking.2: Making several possible cases under the same condition
x-m-e3-05.prereq.0: Knows which length each of a circle's diameter and radius measures (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the information that is absolutely needed to find the radius of one cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find what has not yet been told in the problem that could connect to the length of one cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.hint.1: Cross out one piece of information and check one by one whether you can still decide the size of the cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.o.a: How many cm the height (depth) of the box is
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.r.a: The height of the box has nothing to do with the width of the cookies seen from above. Think about which length connects to the size of the cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.o.b: Whether the cookies are touching with no gaps
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.r.b: Only if the cookies are touching and the ends reach the walls does the length of the box connect to the size of the cookies.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.o.c: How many cm the width of the box is
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.r.c: You need to know the length of the row the cookies are in to work out the length of one cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.o.d: The time it took to bake one cookie
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.r.d: Time is not information that decides the size of a cookie.
x-m-e3-05.s.s1.explain: Only if the 3 cookies are touching in a row with no gaps and both ends reach the walls does the width of the box equal the sum of the diameters of all 3 cookies. The height of the box and the baking time have nothing to do with the radius.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the width of the box is 60 cm, the cookies are touching with no gaps, and both ends reach the walls. What is the radius of one cookie in cm?
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.hint.0: First say how many cm the diameters of the 3 cookies add up to.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.hint.1: After you find the diameter of one cookie, use the relationship between the radius and the diameter one more time.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.r.a: This only found the diameter of one cookie. Check again that the radius is the length from the center of the circle to its edge.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.r.b: This choice found the diameter from the total of the diameters of the 3 cookies and then went on to think that the radius is half of it.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.r.c: You may have divided 60 by 2 instead of by the number of cookies, 3. Count again how many cookies are in the row.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.r.d: This is the value you get by dividing 60 by 4. Find again in the sentence how many cookies there are.
x-m-e3-05.s.s2.explain: The diameters of the 3 cookies add up to 60 cm, so the diameter is 20 cm, and the radius is half of the diameter, 10 cm.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.prompt: You want to put cookies of the same size in a row in the same box (width 60 cm) with no gaps and with both ends touching the walls. When the number of cookies is at least 2 and at most 6, make 3 cases with different numbers of cookies and write the radius of the cookies each time. (You may write the radius as a decimal.)
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.hint.0: Pick a number of cookies, then first think about what diameter makes that many diameters add up to 60 cm.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.hint.1: After changing the diameter you found into a radius, check again whether all the diameters add up to 60 cm.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.ok.c1: The number of cookies is a natural number from 2 to 6.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Write the number of cookies as a natural number from 2 to 6.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.ok.c2: The diameters of the cookies add up to 60 cm.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.fail.c2: The diameters of the cookies do not add up to 60 cm. Check the diameter and the radius again.
x-m-e3-05.s.s3.explain: With 2 cookies the radius is 15 cm, with 3 it is 10 cm, with 5 it is 6 cm, and with 6 it is 5 cm. The more cookies there are, the smaller the radius gets.

x-m-e3-06.title: If All Four Angles Are Right Angles, Is It Always a Square?
x-m-e3-06.goal: Test a generalized claim with a counterexample, and use the definitions of shapes to judge the relationships between shapes.
x-m-e3-06.material: A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles. A square is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles and whose four sides are all the same length. Harin said, 'Every quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles is a square!'
x-m-e3-06.thinking.1: Reasoning about the relationships between shapes from their definitions
x-m-e3-06.thinking.2: Judging in which cases a claim is wrong
x-m-e3-06.prereq.0: Can say what a right angle is, and name the sides and angles of a quadrilateral (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.prompt: How can you check whether what Harin said is always right?
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.hint.0: Say what kind of quadrilateral must not exist for Harin's statement to be right.
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.hint.1: In the definition of a square, find the condition other than 'right angle.'
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.o.a: Draw several squares and measure whether the angles are right angles
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.r.a: A square is already a shape that fits Harin's statement. Think about whether this is a way to find cases where the statement is wrong.
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.o.b: Gather more friends who agree with Harin
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.r.b: The number of people who agree is not evidence that the statement is always right.
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.o.c: Look for a quadrilateral that has right angles but sides of different lengths
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.r.c: This choice thought about how the word 'always' is broken by even a single example that does not fit.
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.o.d: Measure whether the biggest quadrilateral is a square
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.r.d: Size has nothing to do with the name of a shape. Test which part of the definition other quadrilaterals might differ in.
x-m-e3-06.s.s1.explain: The word 'every' is broken by even one example that does not fit. If you find a quadrilateral whose four angles are right angles but whose four sides are not the same length, you can show that Harin's statement is wrong.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 rectangles of different sizes whose four angles are all right angles but that are not squares. Choose the length and width (cm) as natural numbers from 1 to 20, and make the length longer than the width.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether all four sides can be the same length if you choose the length and the width to be different.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether the lengths you chose fit the conditions (natural numbers from 1 to 20, the length is longer).
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The length and the width are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the length and the width as natural numbers from 1 to 20.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The length is longer than the width, so the four sides are not all the same length.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The length must be longer than the width. If the length and the width are the same, it becomes a square.
x-m-e3-06.s.s2.explain: A rectangle with a different length and width, like length 6 cm and width 3 cm, or length 8 cm and width 5 cm, has four right angles but is not a square. If the length and the width are the same, it becomes a square.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.prompt: In light of the definitions above, how can you judge the statement 'A square can be called a rectangle'?
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.hint.0: Check one by one whether a square has every condition given in the definition of a rectangle.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think about the direction of '~ can be called ~': which way does the statement go?
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.o.a: Wrong. A square has sides of the same length, so it is a different shape.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.r.a: Think about whether having one more condition, 'the sides are the same length,' takes it outside the definition of a rectangle.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.o.b: A square is not a rectangle, and a rectangle is not a square.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.r.b: This treats the two shapes as completely separate. Check in the definition what the four angles of a square are like.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.o.c: Every rectangle is a square, so they are the same shape.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.r.c: This is the same as Harin's first claim. Test this idea with the examples you made earlier.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.o.d: Right. A square is also a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles.
x-m-e3-06.s.s3.explain: The four angles of a square are all right angles, so a square meets the definition of a rectangle. So a square can be called a rectangle. But not every rectangle is a square.

x-m-e3-07.title: 2L 400mL and 2300mL: Whose Water Is More?
x-m-e3-07.goal: Find and fix the error of comparing quantities with different units by their numbers alone, and compare after making the units the same.
x-m-e3-07.material: Subin's water bottle has 2L 400mL of water in it, and Jiho's water bottle has 2300mL of water in it. The two friends talk about whose water is more.
x-m-e3-07.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a conversation
x-m-e3-07.thinking.1: Explaining the reason for the error using units
x-m-e3-07.thinking.2: Making and checking amounts that fit the conditions yourself
x-m-e3-07.prereq.0: Knows that L and mL are units for measuring the amount of water, and that 1L equals 1000mL (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in the two friends' conversation that is hard to believe.
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.line.0: Subin: My water bottle at home has 2L 400mL of water in it.
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.line.1: Jiho: My water bottle at home has 2300mL of water in it.
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.line.2: Subin: 400 is less than 2300, so Jiho's water is more.
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.line.3: Jiho: Right, the bigger number is more.
x-m-e3-07.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 4 are wrong. 400 is the number in the mL part, and 2300 is the total mL. You must not compare numbers with different units as they are. If you change 2L 400mL to mL, it is 2400mL, so Subin's water is more.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different amounts that are less than Subin's water (2L 400mL) and more than Jiho's water (2300mL). Write each as some L and some mL. (The mL part is a natural number from 0 to 999.)
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.hint.0: Change both Subin's and Jiho's water to mL and think about the numbers that fit between the two numbers.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write the mL number you chose again as L and mL, and check that it fits the conditions.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The L part and the mL part are written properly.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the L part and the mL part as natural numbers, and the mL part must be from 0 to 999.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.ok.c2: It is more than Jiho's water (2300mL).
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not more than Jiho's water. Change to the same unit and compare.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.ok.c3: It is less than Subin's water (2400mL).
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.fail.c3: It is not less than Subin's water. Change to the same unit and compare.
x-m-e3-07.s.s2.explain: Amounts like 2L 310mL, 2L 350mL, and 2L 399mL, which add 301mL to 399mL to 2L, all fit the conditions.
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.prompt: Tell Subin and Jiho whose water is more, and write how they should compare.
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.hint.0: Decide on one unit to use for both, and rewrite the two amounts.
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put the two changed numbers side by side and say which one is bigger.
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually say the numbers you got by writing both amounts in the same unit?
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words why you cannot compare by the numbers alone when the units are different?
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.model.0: You have to change L to mL and compare. 2L 400mL is 2400mL, which is more than 2300mL. Subin's water is more.
x-m-e3-07.s.s3.model.1: When the units are different, you cannot go by the numbers alone. If you put both in mL, it is 2400mL and 2300mL, so Subin's, at 2400mL, is more.

x-m-e3-08.title: Different Ways to Put Apples and Tangerines in a Bag
x-m-e3-08.goal: Make the conditions with mixed kg and g the same unit, make several ways, and explain the relationship: how many tangerines weigh the same as one apple.
x-m-e3-08.material: The bag itself weighs 500 g. One apple weighs 300 g, and one tangerine weighs 100 g. You want to put apples and tangerines in this bag so that the weight including the bag is at least 1 kg 900 g and at most 2 kg.
x-m-e3-08.thinking.0: Interpreting the conditions by making the units the same
x-m-e3-08.thinking.1: Finding several ways that meet the conditions
x-m-e3-08.prereq.1: Can add and multiply with units of g
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.prompt: You put 2 apples and 5 tangerines in the bag. How much does it weigh including the bag?
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.hint.0: Find the weights of the apples, the tangerines, and the bag, and write them all in g.
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find the total, then write it again as kg and g.
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.r.a: You may have added only the weight of the fruit and left out the weight of the bag. Read the problem's 'including the bag' again.
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.r.c: You may have counted both the apples and the tangerines as 300 g. Check the weight of one tangerine again.
x-m-e3-08.s.s1.explain: 2 apples are 600 g, 5 tangerines are 500 g, and the bag is 500 g, so all together it is 1600 g, that is, 1 kg 600 g. This weight falls short of 1 kg 900 g.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.prompt: Put in at least 1 apple and at least 1 tangerine so that the weight including the bag is at least 1 kg 900 g and at most 2 kg. Make 3 ways with different numbers of apples.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.hint.0: First change 1 kg 900 g and 2 kg to g and set the range for the weight.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a number of apples, add the bag and the apples together, then work out how many more tangerines you need to put in to land in the range.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.ok.c1: You put in at least 1 apple and at least 1 tangerine.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Write both the apples and the tangerines as natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is at least 1 kg 900 g.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The total weight falls short of 1 kg 900 g. Change everything to g and add again.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The total weight is heavier than 2 kg. Change everything to g and add again.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.explain: 1 apple and 11 tangerines, 2 apples and 8 tangerines, 3 apples and 5 tangerines, and 4 apples and 2 tangerines are all 1900 g including the bag. Each time there is 1 more apple, if you take away 3 tangerines, the weight stays the same.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare in g how many tangerines weigh the same as one apple.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you put in 1 more apple, take out ... tangerines
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason using the weights of the apple and the tangerine (300 g and 100 g)?
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.because.model.0: If you put in 1 more apple, you have to take out 3 tangerines. 1 apple is 300 g and 1 tangerine is 100 g, so it weighs the same as 3 tangerines.
x-m-e3-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Take out 3 tangerines. One apple weighs the same as three tangerines (300 g).

x-m-e3-09.title: Did the Village with the Most Pictures Pick the Most Apples?
x-m-e3-09.goal: Find out, by revising your judgment as information is revealed, that you must not just count the pictures in a picture graph and that you need to know the number one picture stands for.
x-m-e3-09.material: The apple harvests of three villages (가, 나, 다) are shown in a picture graph. The information is revealed one step at a time. At each step, choose the best idea given what you know right now.
x-m-e3-09.thinking.0: Revising your judgment with new information
x-m-e3-09.thinking.1: Reading data based on the number each picture stands for
x-m-e3-09.thinking.2: Telling apart the number of pictures from the actual amount and arguing against a claim
x-m-e3-09.prereq.0: Has heard that in a picture graph, one picture stands for a set number (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.prompt: Look at the information one piece at a time and see whether there is any judgment you should change.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first check the numbers that the big picture and the small picture stand for.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.hint.1: Change the pictures of each village into a number of boxes, write them down, and compare them side by side.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The picture graph has big pictures and small pictures. Village 가 is drawn with 2 big pictures, and Village 나 is drawn with 1 big picture and 9 small pictures. It is not yet known how many boxes one picture stands for.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which village picked the most apples?
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.after: If you do not know how many boxes one picture stands for, it is hard to compare exactly. You can guess that a big picture stands for a bigger amount, but you need to check.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This choice guessed that a big picture stands for a bigger amount than a small picture.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This choice only looked at the number of pictures being large. Think about whether a big picture and a small picture are the same amount.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is hard to decide right now
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This choice pointed out that you do not know the number one picture stands for.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.1.info: New information: 1 big picture stands for 10 boxes, and 1 small picture stands for 1 box.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, which has more, Village 가 or Village 나?
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.1.after: Village 가 is 20 boxes, and Village 나 is 10+9=19 boxes. Village 나 has more pictures, but Village 가 has the bigger harvest.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: The data for Village 다 arrived late. Village 다 is drawn with 2 big pictures and 2 small pictures.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which of the three villages picked the most apples?
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.st.2.after: Village 다 is 20+2=22 boxes. 22 boxes is more than 20 boxes and 19 boxes, so with the new information you have to revise the earlier judgment that Village 가 has the most.
x-m-e3-09.s.s1.reflect: Counting pictures alone could not give a conclusion, and when the data for the new village came in, the earlier conclusion changed. Think back to which information, at which step, made you change your judgment.
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.prompt: A friend says, 'The village with more pictures has the bigger harvest.' Use the example of these villages to tell your friend.
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.hint.0: Compare whether the village with the most pictures and the village with the most boxes are the same.
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.hint.1: Explain by writing side by side the number of pictures and the number of boxes for the two villages you compared.
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Having more pictures does not mean ...
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the numbers of boxes of Villages 가, 나, and 다 using numbers?
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words that the big picture and the small picture stand for different numbers?
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.model.0: Even with many pictures, they can add up to less if they are small pictures. Village 나 has 10 pictures, but it is 1 big picture (10 boxes) and 9 small pictures (9 boxes), so 19 boxes, and Village 가 has 2 big pictures, so 20 boxes.
x-m-e3-09.s.s2.model.1: Each picture stands for a different number of boxes, so you must not just count them. Village 나 has 10 pictures but 19 boxes, and Village 가 has 2 pictures but 20 boxes.

x-m-e3-10.title: Showing the Books Three Groups Read in a Picture Graph
x-m-e3-10.goal: Make data that fits the sum and the ranges within the conditions on the values the big picture and the small picture stand for, and say how to show that data in a picture graph.
x-m-e3-10.material: You want to show the number of books that three groups (가, 나, 다) read in a picture graph. 1 big picture stands for 10 books, and 1 small picture stands for 1 book. The three groups read 57 books in all.
x-m-e3-10.thinking.0: Making data that meets several conditions at the same time
x-m-e3-10.thinking.1: Deciding the number of pictures to match place value
x-m-e3-10.prereq.0: Understands the rule that in a picture graph, the big picture stands for 10 books and the small picture stands for 1 book (Grade 3 level)
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.prompt: When Group 가 read 31 books, how many big pictures and how many small pictures should you draw in the picture graph?
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.hint.0: First group 31 into as many groups of 10 books as you can.
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many small pictures the books left over after grouping can be shown with.
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.r.a: You may have read the two digits of 31 in the wrong order. Check again how many books one big picture stands for.
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.r.b: You may have missed that there are small pictures. Check again how many books one big picture stands for.
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.r.c: This choice split 31 into how many tens and how many ones and changed them into numbers of pictures.
x-m-e3-10.s.s1.explain: 31 books is 3 groups of 10 books and 1 book. So you show it with 3 big pictures and 1 small picture.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.prompt: Decide the number of books for each group so that the three groups read 57 books in all. Group 가 has 3 big pictures, Group 나 has 2 big pictures, and Group 다 has no big pictures and only small pictures (at least 1 book). Make 3 different cases.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.hint.0: First write the range of books that Group 가 and Group 나 can read, using their numbers of big pictures.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.hint.1: After you decide the numbers of books for 가 and 나, subtract their sum from 57 to find the number of books for Group 다, and check that it fits the conditions.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of books as a natural number.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.fail.c2: For 3 big pictures, Group 가 must have at least 30 and at most 39 books.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.fail.c3: For 2 big pictures, Group 나 must have at least 20 and at most 29 books.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.ok.c4: Group 다 has only small pictures.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.fail.c4: Group 다 has no big pictures, so it must have at least 1 and at most 9 books.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.ok.c5: The three groups have 57 books in all.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.fail.c5: The books of the three groups do not add up to 57.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.explain: For example, 30, 20, and 7 books, or 31, 22, and 4 books, both add up to 57. The 5 big pictures of 가 and 나 are 50 books, so the single books of 가 and 나 plus the books of Group 다 must add up to 7.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the cases you made, and write how you would draw Groups 가, 나, and 다 in a picture graph, using numbers of big pictures and small pictures.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.hint.0: In the case you picked, split Group 가's number of books into groups of 10 books and single books.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.hint.1: Decide the numbers of pictures for Group 나 and Group 다 the same way.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Group 가 has 3 big pictures and ... small pictures
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In the case you picked, do the books the big pictures and small pictures stand for add up to each group's number of books?
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check again that the books of the three groups add up to 57?
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.model.0: Group 가's 31 books are drawn as 3 big pictures and 1 small picture, Group 나's 22 books as 2 big pictures and 2 small pictures, and Group 다's 4 books as 4 small pictures.
x-m-e3-10.s.s2.because.model.1: Draw 3 big pictures and 5 small pictures for Group 가 (35 books), 2 big pictures and 0 small pictures for Group 나 (20 books), and 2 small pictures for Group 다 (2 books).
